3. The middle section of Fanny's monologue about annuities: preserved well.

4. A few notable cuts/changes:

- The third paragraph in source: "It was very well known that no affection was ever supposed to exist between the children of any man by different marriages; and why was he to ruin himself, and their poor little Harry, by giving away all his money to his half sisters?" — this ironic narratorial sentence is absent/compressed. The draft replaces it with a shortened paraphrase.

- "To be sure it would." exchange (the "To be sure it would" beat after "very convenient addition") is omitted — minor but cuts one step of the comic degradation.

- The annuity speech: "and it was the more unkind in my father, because, otherwise, the money would have been entirely at my mother's disposal, without any restriction whatever" — this detail is dropped. It's a small character-revealing moment but not a major signature.

- Mr. Dashwood's reasoning about occasional gifts: "because they would only enlarge their style of living if they felt sure of a larger income, and would not be sixpence the richer for it at the end of the year" — this is absent from the draft. It's a rhetorically distinctive phrase ("not be sixpence the richer") that shows Dashwood has been fully won over.

- Fanny's "Only conceive how comfortable they will be! Five hundred a year!" speech: "Their housekeeping will be nothing at all. They will have no carriage, no horses, and hardly any servants; they will keep no company, and can have no expenses of any kind!" — the draft condenses this: "Housekeeping nothing at all. No carriage, no horses, hardly any servants; no company, no expenses of any kind!" — the parallel structure and subject-verb construction is slightly flattened but the content is mostly there.

- The italicized emphases (_let_, _that_, _really_, _they_, _them_) are mostly stripped. These are signature elements of Austen's ironic rendering of Fanny's speech.

- "I clearly understand it now" — omitted from the draft's version of Mr. Dashwood's final capitulation speech. Minor.

- The "To be sure it would" beat — completely absent.

The most notable issues are: (1) loss of italicized emphases throughout the dialogue (signature of Austen's ironic voice), (2) the "not be sixpence the richer" line, and (3) slight compression of the narratorial irony in paragraph 3.

None of these rise to high severity since no pre-pass signatures were tagged. Let me assess:

- The italics stripping across dialogue is a medium-level voice flattening — these emphases are characteristic Austenian irony markers.
- The "sixpence the richer" omission is medium — distinctively phrased.
- The "To be sure it would" omission is low.
